                 HEAD / HUB

                  │
                  ▼

                  │
                  ▼
             ROUTINE 20

                  │
                  ▼
             RETURN TO HUB
                  │

    That gives us a very explicit beginning-to-end lifecycle.

    But I would change one part of your idea

    I wouldn't make unused routines literally empty pass-through files unless there is a particular reason to do so.

    Instead, we can establish a 20-slot architecture where every program has 20 possible routine positions, but unused positions contain a tiny, standardized pass-through routine.

    Something like:

    #!/usr/bin/env bash

# ============================================================
# UNUSED ROUTINE
# ============================================================

exit 0

    That is essentially a NOP — "no operation."

    The Hub can therefore always execute:

    01 → 02 → 03 → 04 → ... → 20

    without needing to know whether a particular slot is being used.

    That's actually quite elegant.

    And Routine 20 has a special job

    I would make Routine 20 the formal termination routine.

    It wouldn't just be another empty slot.

    It could perform things such as:

    ROUTINE 20 — FINALIZE / STOP
│
├── Confirm final operation completed
├── Write completion information to log
├── Close/clean temporary resources
├── Report SUCCESS
└── Return 0

    Then the Hub receives that successful return and performs the actual final stop.

    So we have:

    Routine 20 says:

    "The application's work is finished."

    The Hub says:

    "Understood. The application is now stopping."

    That separation is useful.

    There's also a nice safety feature here

    We can make the Hub refuse to consider the program successfully completed unless the final routine returns success.

    For example:

    Routine 19
   │
   ▼
Routine 20 — FINALIZE
   │
   ├── SUCCESS → Hub → STOP
   │
   └── FAILURE → Hub → ERROR / STOP

    So there isn't an ambiguous situation where the program simply disappears because it reached the end of a script.

    The generic framework could therefore establish this rule

    Every application has:

    HEAD / HUB
     │
     ├── Routine 01
     ├── Routine 02
     ├── Routine 03
     ├── ...
     ├── Routine 19
     │
     └── Routine 20 — FINALIZE

    Maximum: 20 routines.

    An application might use only five:

    01 = Receive
02 = Validate
03 = Process
04 = Output
05 = Finalize

    and routines 06–19 are standardized pass-throughs.

    Or another application could use all twenty.

    One refinement I'd recommend

    I would reserve Routine 20 exclusively for termination/finalization rather than allowing an application to use it for ordinary work.

    That gives the generic framework a permanent rule:

    Routine 20 always means "we are finishing."

    That makes the architecture much easier to understand years from now — including when we're looking at some completely different program that we build six months from now.

    And I think this fits very nicely with your larger idea of a generic Bash application framework: the launcher doesn't need to understand the individual program. It only needs to understand the standard structure, the Hub, the routine sequence, the return codes, and the finalization convention.

│   └── ...

    • There is exactly one designated finalization routine.

    • Required environment information is available.

    • The program isn't accidentally pointing at a different program's routines.

    • The program's internal structure agrees with its manifest.

[OK] Routine 03

[OK] Routine 07

  96. ChatGPT said:

    Yes. I’ll make this a proper foundational paper rather than merely documentation for the Wizard. I’ll also include appendices/addenda that distinguish the established ideas we are building upon from the synthesis we are proposing.

    The Checkpointed Routine Method

    An Architecture for Human-Readable, Independently Verifiable, Failure-Safe Automation

    A philosophical and architectural foundation for the Session Preservation Wizard

    Version 1.0 — Foundational Draft

    Abstract

    Complex automation frequently becomes difficult not because any individual operation is particularly complicated, but because too many operations, assumptions, responsibilities, and recovery decisions become entangled within a single program.

    This paper proposes an architectural method called the Checkpointed Routine Method.

    The method organizes automation as a sequence of small, independently understandable routines controlled by a simple orchestration layer, or Hub. Each routine has a clearly defined responsibility and follows a common contract:

    1. Input — What information does the routine receive?

    2. Precheck — What must be true before it begins?

    3. Action — What does it actually do?

    4. Verify — How does it establish that the action succeeded?

    5. Return — How does it communicate success or failure?

    A successful routine permits progression to the next checkpoint. A failed routine stops the process without attempting to conceal, reinterpret, or silently repair the failure.

    The method further introduces several related principles:

    • preservation before transformation;

    • independent verification of consequential operations;

    • separation of original and derived artifacts;

    • progressive commitment;

    • delayed destructive operations;

    • explicit provenance;

    • single responsibility for routines;

    • a deliberately simple controller;

    • and human-readable program structure.

    The paper argues that this architecture is particularly useful for systems in which loss of data, ambiguous state, or incorrect claims of success are more dangerous than stopping.

    A further observation is proposed: the explicit structure of the method may make it useful not only for human programmers but also as a collaboration language between humans and AI systems. By making inputs, assumptions, actions, verification criteria, and failure semantics explicit, the architecture reduces ambiguity in both programming and technical communication.

    The method is demonstrated through the design of a Session Preservation Wizard whose purpose is to preserve original browser captures, create separate publication copies, verify repository and webpage states independently, establish provenance-preserving links between them, and perform destructive cleanup only after successful verification.

    The Checkpointed Routine Method does not claim to replace established software-engineering disciplines. Rather, it proposes a practical synthesis of structured programming, defensive automation, verification, provenance management, and human-readable orchestration.

    1. Introduction

    Automation is often described as a way of making complicated work easier.

    There is an important qualification:

    Automation can make complicated work easier to perform while making the underlying program harder to understand.

    This happens when individual operations are combined into increasingly large procedures.

    A program may begin with a simple sequence:

    copy something
verify it
publish it
verify publication
delete the original

    Over time, additional requirements appear:

    check whether the drive exists
check whether the source exists
avoid overwriting existing material
handle network failure
retry publication
verify remote state
preserve the original filename
create a web-compatible derivative
verify the derivative
create a link
verify the link
clean temporary files
clean the source
report final state

    The natural temptation is to place all of these decisions into one increasingly sophisticated program.

    The result can become difficult to inspect, difficult to troubleshoot, and difficult to modify safely.

    The Checkpointed Routine Method takes the opposite approach.

    Instead of asking:

    How can we make one program intelligent enough to handle everything?

    it asks:

    How can we make each individual operation so clear that the controller does not need to be intelligent?

    This leads to a fundamental design principle:

    Make the routines boring.

    “Boring” here is a positive engineering property.

    A boring routine has:

    • one responsibility;

    • visible assumptions;

    • predictable inputs;

    • explicit verification;

    • explicit failure;

    • limited side effects;

    • and an understandable return condition.

    The complexity is moved from hidden internal decision-making into an explicit sequence of checkpoints.

    2. Historical Foundation

    The philosophy developed here has strong relationships to established ideas in software engineering, particularly structured programming and modular design.

    Structured programming emphasized the importance of understandable control flow and discouraged arbitrary jumps through a program.

    Modular programming emphasized separation of concerns and the division of large systems into manageable components.

    Procedural programming provided a natural model in which a controlling procedure could call smaller procedures that performed particular operations.

    The Checkpointed Routine Method builds upon these traditions.

    It does not claim that the underlying concepts are new.

    Its proposed contribution is instead a particular operational synthesis:

    simple controller
       +
single-purpose routines
       +
explicit contracts
       +
independent verification
       +
controlled commitment
       +
delayed destruction

    The result is intended to be useful in situations where reliability and recoverability matter more than minimizing the number of lines of code.

    3. The Central Philosophy

    The central philosophy can be stated in several rules.

    Rule 1 — One routine should have one job

    A routine should perform one identifiable responsibility.

    For example:

    VERIFY WEBPAGE

    should verify the webpage.

    It should not also:

    • modify the Library;

    • delete the archive;

    • repair the webpage;

    • rename files;

    • or decide whether a failed webpage should be ignored.

    This makes the routine easier to understand and easier to replace.

    Rule 2 — The Hub controls; routines perform

    The controller should not contain the implementation details of every operation.

    Its responsibility is primarily:

    CALL ROUTINE
CHECK RETURN
CONTINUE OR STOP

    Conceptually:

    START
  ↓
CALL 01
  ↓
SUCCESS?
 ├── NO → STOP
 └── YES
       ↓
     CALL 02
       ↓
     SUCCESS?
      ├── NO → STOP
      └── YES
            ↓
           ...

    The Hub therefore becomes an orchestrator, not a giant worker routine.

    Rule 3 — A routine should verify its own work

    A command reporting success is not necessarily equivalent to the desired result existing.

    For example:

    git push

    reporting success establishes one fact.

    It does not necessarily establish every fact we care about.

    The Checkpointed Routine Method therefore distinguishes:

    "I attempted the operation."

    from:

    "The desired resulting state exists."

    This distinction becomes especially important for networked systems.

    4. The Five-Part Routine Contract

    Every routine should ideally be understandable through the same five-part contract.

    4.1 Input

    What does the routine receive?

    For example:

    SESSION_NAME
PAGE_URL

    The input should be explicit.

    A routine should not depend upon mysterious state that exists only because another routine happened to create it.

    4.2 Precheck

    What must be true before the routine begins?

    Examples:

    Does the repository exist?

Does the source session exist?

Does the required file exist?

Is the repository clean?

Has the required URL been supplied?

    Prechecks prevent a routine from attempting an operation under conditions for which it was not designed.

    4.3 Action

    What does the routine actually do?

    The action should be narrow and explicit.

    For example:

    copy the prepared webpage into the Web repository

    rather than:

    prepare, publish, repair, verify, and clean the webpage

    4.4 Verification

    How does the routine establish that the action worked?

    This is the most important distinction between an ordinary procedure and a checkpointed routine.

    The routine should ask:

    What observable condition constitutes success?

    Examples include:

    the destination exists

the expected file exists

the expected directory exists

the remote commit matches the local commit

the webpage returns HTTP 200

the returned content contains HTML

    4.5 Return

    The routine communicates the result to its controller.

    The basic contract can be:

    0 = SUCCESS
non-zero = FAILURE

    This creates a simple language between the Hub and its routines.

    The Hub does not need to understand the internal details.

    It only needs to understand:

    success

    or:

    failure

    5. Checkpointed Execution

    The architecture can be represented as:

                     ┌─────────────────┐
                 │     ROUTINE     │
                 └────────┬────────┘
                          ↓
                       ACTION
                          ↓
                       VERIFY
                          ↓
                 ┌────────┴────────┐
                 │                 │
              SUCCESS           FAILURE
                 │                 │
                 ↓                 ↓
          NEXT ROUTINE           STOP

    The important characteristic is that failure is not merely an error message.

    Failure is a control-flow event.

    It prevents subsequent operations from assuming something that has not been established.

    This is particularly important when later operations are destructive.

    For example:

    VERIFY WEBPAGE
      ↓
   FAILURE
      ↓
DO NOT DELETE ARCHIVE

    The failed verification therefore protects recoverability.

    6. Independent Verification

    One of the most important concepts in the method is that apparently similar statements can represent different facts.

    Consider three statements:

    The upload command succeeded.

The repository contains the files.

The public webpage can be retrieved.

    These are not identical claims.

    A system can therefore use separate checkpoints:

    PUSH
  ↓
VERIFY REPOSITORY
  ↓
VERIFY SERVICE

    This is the philosophy behind the three-stage Web verification sequence:

    Stage 1 — Push

    "I sent it."

    Stage 2 — Repository verification

    "The repository contains it."

    Stage 3 — Webpage verification

    "The published service actually serves it."

    The distinction is valuable because distributed systems frequently contain intermediate states.

    A successful command does not necessarily imply successful propagation through every layer of a system.

    7. Progressive Commitment

    A second central principle is progressive commitment.

    The system should move from easily reversible actions toward increasingly irreversible actions.

    Conceptually:

    RECEIVE
   ↓
VERIFY
   ↓
PRESERVE
   ↓
TRANSFORM
   ↓
PUBLISH
   ↓
VERIFY
   ↓
LINK
   ↓
VERIFY
   ↓
DESTROY TEMPORARY COPY
   ↓
DESTROY ORIGINAL INPUT

    The system therefore postpones destructive operations until the evidence supporting them is strongest.

    This produces a useful general rule:

    The more irreversible the operation, the stronger the preceding verification should be.

    8. Preservation Before Transformation

    The original artifact and a derivative should not automatically be treated as the same thing.

    In the Session Preservation Wizard, the original Edge capture is deliberately preserved:

    Original Title.html
Original Title_files/

    The Web system receives a derived representation:

    index.html
Original Title_files/

    The distinction is fundamental.

    The original artifact is evidence of what the source system produced.

    The Web copy is an adaptation intended for a different environment.

    Therefore:

    Preserve the primary artifact; derive the publication artifact.

    This prevents publication requirements from contaminating the preservation copy.

    9. Provenance

    Once original and derived artifacts are separated, their relationship must be made explicit.

    The architecture therefore introduces a navigation artifact:

    READ_EPISODE.html

    which points from the preserved Library record to the verified published webpage.

    Conceptually:

    ORIGINAL ARTIFACT
      │
      │ preserved
      ▼
   LIBRARY
      │
      │ navigation relationship
      ▼
PUBLISHED WEBPAGE

    This is preferable to modifying the original artifact simply to insert a link.

    The original remains original.

    The relationship is stored separately.

    This principle generalizes beyond browser captures.

    It can apply to:

    • scientific datasets;

    • manuscripts;

    • photographs;

    • recordings;

    • source documents;

    • software builds;

    • experimental records;

    • and research sessions.

    10. The Archive as a State Machine

    The temporary archive provides an interesting example of a broader principle: sometimes physical or filesystem state can serve as a simple state representation.

    Before successful processing:

    GitHub_Session_Archive/
└── Episode-Whatever/

    After successful processing:

    GitHub_Session_Archive/
└── [empty]

    The archive therefore answers a simple operational question:

    Is there still work waiting to be completed?

    No database is necessarily required to answer that question.

    The filesystem state itself communicates the answer.

    This suggests a broader design principle:

    Do not create an additional state-management system when the existing state of the artifacts already expresses the required information reliably.

    This principle must, of course, be applied cautiously. A filesystem is not a universal replacement for a database. It is useful here because the state being represented is deliberately simple.

    11. Failure Semantics

    A critical philosophical decision is what the system does when something goes wrong.

    The Checkpointed Routine Method favors:

    FAIL → STOP → PRESERVE

    rather than:

    FAIL → GUESS → REPAIR → CONTINUE

    There are systems where automated recovery is appropriate.

    The present architecture deliberately favors conservatism when data preservation is involved.

    If the webpage cannot be verified, the system does not conclude:

    "It probably worked."

    It concludes:

    "The required condition has not been established."

    That distinction is essential.

    12. The Principle of Non-Repairing Verification

    A verification routine should normally verify rather than repair.

    For example:

    Routine 09

    checks whether the webpage is available.

    If it fails, it should not secretly:

    • alter the repository;

    • rewrite the webpage;

    • change the URL;

    • delete anything;

    • or manufacture a different interpretation of success.

    Instead:

    VERIFY
  ↓
FAIL
  ↓
REPORT
  ↓
STOP

    This produces a clearer diagnostic history.

    The failure remains visible.

    The system's state remains recoverable.

    Human intervention can then determine the appropriate response.

    13. Human-Readable Automation

    The method treats human comprehension as an engineering requirement.

    A program should not merely be executable.

    It should be inspectable.

    A programmer encountering a routine months later should be able to answer quickly:

    What is this?
What does it need?
What does it check?
What does it change?
How does it know it worked?
What happens if it fails?

    This is why extensive structural comments can be valuable.

    The comments are not merely explanations of syntax.

    They establish architectural boundaries.

    For example:

    # 09D — TRY THE PAGE

    communicates that the following block has a particular conceptual responsibility.

    The program therefore becomes partially self-documenting.

    14. Replaceability

    Single-purpose routines have another important property:

    They can be replaced.

    Suppose GitHub Pages were eventually replaced by another publishing service.

    Ideally, the architecture would not require redesigning the entire system.

    The Web verification routine could be replaced or adapted.

    The surrounding contract could remain:

    INPUT:
    SESSION_NAME
    PAGE_URL

ACTION:
    verify published webpage

RETURN:
    0 = success
    non-zero = failure

    The Hub does not need to know how verification is implemented.

    This is one of the practical benefits of separating orchestration from implementation.

    15. The Hub as a Control Language

    The Hub can be extremely simple:

    CALL 01
IF FAILURE STOP

CALL 02
IF FAILURE STOP

CALL 03
IF FAILURE STOP

...

CALL 13
IF FAILURE STOP

END

    At first glance this may seem almost too simple.

    That simplicity is intentional.

    The Hub becomes a kind of control language.

    It expresses:

    first this
then this
then this
but only if the previous operation succeeded

    The routines contain the operational knowledge.

    The Hub contains the sequencing knowledge.

    This separation reduces coupling.

    16. A Routine as a Contract

    The routine can therefore be viewed not merely as code, but as a contract.

    For example:

    ROUTINE 09

INPUT:
    SESSION_NAME

PRECONDITION:
    Web repository has already been verified.

ACTION:
    Request the expected public webpage.

VERIFICATION:
    Obtain a successful HTTP response containing HTML.

SUCCESS:
    Return 0.

FAILURE:
    Return non-zero and change nothing.

    The executable code becomes an implementation of the contract.

    This has implications for both human and AI-assisted programming.

    17. The AI Collaboration Dimension

    One of the more interesting consequences of the method is its usefulness as a communication framework between a human and an AI system.

    AI-assisted programming can fail when the human and AI hold different implicit assumptions about:

    • what a routine is supposed to do;

    • what constitutes success;

    • what may be modified;

    • what must remain untouched;

    • what failure means;

    • or when destructive actions are permissible.

    The Five-Part Routine Contract makes these assumptions explicit.

    For example:

    INPUT
PRECHECK
ACTION
VERIFY
RETURN

    provides a compact shared vocabulary.

    A human can tell an AI:

    "Design Routine 08. Its responsibility is only to verify the Web repository."

    The AI can then reason within a constrained architectural space.

    The human can inspect whether the proposed routine violates the contract.

    This does not eliminate mistakes.

    It makes mistakes easier to identify.

    The architecture therefore has the potential to function as an operational meta-language for human-AI collaboration.

    That proposition should be treated as a subject for further investigation rather than as an established scientific result.

    18. Why Explicitness Helps AI

    Human programmers routinely infer context from experience.

    An experienced programmer may understand that:

    git push succeeded

    does not necessarily mean:

    the website works

    An AI may also understand this distinction, but explicit contracts make the intended distinction much less ambiguous.

    The architecture therefore encourages statements such as:

    Routine 07:
    push

Routine 08:
    verify repository

Routine 09:
    verify webpage

    rather than:

    publish session

    The second phrase hides several propositions.

    The first three expose them.

    This suggests a potentially useful research question:

    Can explicit routine contracts improve reliability and mutual understanding in AI-assisted software development?

    The answer should be established experimentally rather than assumed.

    19. Research Provenance

    The philosophy extends beyond software.

    A research archive should ideally distinguish among different epistemic states.

    For example:

    OBSERVATION
     ↓
INTERPRETATION
     ↓
HYPOTHESIS
     ↓
PROPOSED EXPERIMENT
     ↓
RESULT
     ↓
CONCLUSION

    These are not interchangeable.

    A hypothesis should not silently become a fact.

    A proposed experiment should not be represented as a completed experiment.

    A conceptual framework should not automatically be represented as an established scientific theory.

    The archive can preserve these distinctions by preserving the actual development history.

    This is especially important for collaborative human-AI research.

    The conversation itself may contain:

    • questions;

    • assumptions;

    • rejected ideas;

    • definitions;

    • hypotheses;

    • experiments;

    • corrections;

    • and discoveries.

    Preserving the conversation can therefore preserve intellectual provenance that would otherwise disappear when only the final paper is retained.

    20. The Session Preservation Wizard as a Case Study

    The architecture described here is implemented conceptually by a thirteen-stage workflow.

    01 Receive session
02 Verify thumb drive
03 Archive session
04 Prepare Web copy
05 Push Library
06 Verify Library
07 Push Web
08 Verify Web files
09 Verify actual webpage
10 Create Library link
11 Verify Library link
12 Clean temporary archive
13 Clean thumb drive

    The important feature is not the number thirteen.

    The important feature is the semantic progression.

    20.1 Preservation

    The incoming session is first protected.

    THUMB DRIVE
      ↓
TEMPORARY ARCHIVE

    20.2 Library publication

    The original artifact is placed into the preservation repository.

    ARCHIVE
      ↓
LIBRARY

    The original filename is retained.

    20.3 Web publication

    A separate derivative is placed into the Web repository.

    ARCHIVE
      ↓
WEB WORK
      ↓
WEB REPOSITORY

    The Web copy can use:

    index.html

    without changing the original Library artifact.

    20.4 Verification

    The two repositories are verified independently.

    Then the public webpage is verified independently of the repository.

    Then the Library link is verified.

    20.5 Destruction

    Only after the preceding evidence exists does the system remove:

    TEMPORARY ARCHIVE COPY

    and finally:

    THUMB DRIVE COPY

    The order is itself a safety mechanism.

    21. The Two-Artifact Principle

    The case study demonstrates a broader principle:

    A preservation artifact and a publication artifact may represent the same underlying work without being the same file.

    This distinction is valuable because different environments have different requirements.

    The Library prioritizes:

    fidelity

    The Web copy prioritizes:

    accessibility

    The navigation artifact provides:

    relationship

    The system therefore avoids forcing one file to serve incompatible purposes.

    22. Destruction as a Privileged Operation

    The architecture treats deletion differently from ordinary operations.

    Copying can often be repeated.

    Verification can usually be repeated.

    Deletion may not be reversible.

    Therefore:

    Destructive routines should occur as late as practical and require the strongest available evidence.

    This produces a hierarchy:

    READ
 ↓
COPY
 ↓
VERIFY
 ↓
PUBLISH
 ↓
VERIFY
 ↓
LINK
 ↓
VERIFY
 ↓
DELETE TEMPORARY COPY
 ↓
DELETE ORIGINAL

    Deletion is therefore not merely another routine.

    It is a privileged transition.

    23. The Meaning of "Mission Accomplished"

    The final state should not mean merely:

    "The last command exited successfully."

    It should mean that the defined chain of propositions has been established.

    For the Session Preservation Wizard:

    Original received
        ↓
Original preserved
        ↓
Library verified
        ↓
Web copy verified
        ↓
Webpage verified
        ↓
Library link verified
        ↓
Temporary archive cleaned
        ↓
Original input cleaned

    The final message is therefore a summary of established states.

    The phrase:

    MISSION ACCOMPLISHED

    has meaning because it is downstream of explicit checkpoints.

    24. Limitations

    The method is not a guarantee of correctness.

    Several limitations remain.

    24.1 Verification is only as strong as its criteria

    A test for HTTP 200 does not prove that the webpage is semantically correct.

    A file existing does not prove that its contents are correct.

    A matching Git commit does not prove that the human intended to publish that content.

    Verification must therefore be designed carefully.

    24.2 Independent routines can still share dependencies

    Two routines are not truly independent merely because they are separate scripts.

    If both rely on the same faulty assumption, they may reproduce the same error.

    Independence should therefore be understood in terms of failure modes, not merely file boundaries.

    24.3 Filesystem state has limits

    Using directories as status indicators works well for simple workflows.

    More complicated systems may require:

    • databases;

    • manifests;

    • transaction logs;

    • checksums;

    • signed records;

    • or other persistent state mechanisms.

    The principle is not:

    Never use a database.

    It is:

    Do not introduce additional state machinery unless the problem requires it.

    24.4 Human judgment remains necessary

    A stopped system is not necessarily a solved system.

    The method intentionally favors stopping over guessing.

    Someone must eventually investigate unresolved failures.

    That is a feature rather than a defect when the alternative is silent corruption.

    25. Proposed General Principles

    The philosophy can be summarized as a set of principles.

    Principle 1 — Single Responsibility

    One routine should have one identifiable job.

    Principle 2 — Explicit Contract

    Every routine should clearly define input, preconditions, action, verification, and return.

    Principle 3 — Verification

    Do not confuse an attempted operation with an established result.

    Principle 4 — Independent Checkpoints

    When two successful states are materially different, verify them separately.

    Principle 5 — Progressive Commitment

    Move from reversible actions toward irreversible actions.

    Principle 6 — Preserve Before Transforming

    Protect the primary artifact before creating derivatives.

    Principle 7 — Separate Original and Derived Artifacts

    Do not alter preservation artifacts merely to satisfy publication requirements.

    Principle 8 — Failure Means Stop

    When a required condition is not established, do not silently continue.

    Principle 9 — Verification Does Not Repair

    A verification routine should normally report state rather than alter it.

    Principle 10 — The Hub Controls

    The controller sequences operations but does not perform their internal work.

    Principle 11 — Make the Routines Boring

    Predictability is a reliability feature.

    Principle 12 — Human Comprehension Is an Engineering Requirement

    A program should be understandable by someone who did not write it.

    26. A Compact Formal Model

    The method can be expressed abstractly.

    Let each routine RiR_i have:

    Ri=(Ii,Pi,Ai,Vi,Oi)R_i = (I_i, P_i, A_i, V_i, O_i)

    where:

    • IiI_i = required input;

    • PiP_i = preconditions;

    • AiA_i = action;

    • ViV_i = verification procedure;

    • OiO_i = output/return state.

    The routine succeeds only if:

    Pi=trueP_i = \text{true}

    and after performing AiA_i:

    Vi=trueV_i = \text{true}

    Then:

    Ri→SUCCESSR_i \rightarrow SUCCESS

    Otherwise:

    Ri→FAILURER_i \rightarrow FAILURE

    The controller permits the next routine only when:

    Ri=SUCCESSR_i = SUCCESS

    Therefore:

    R1(SUCCESS)∧R2(SUCCESS)∧...∧Rn(SUCCESS)R_1(SUCCESS) \land R_2(SUCCESS) \land ... \land R_n(SUCCESS)

    is required before the system reaches its terminal success state.

    A destructive operation DD is permitted only after the relevant verification predicates have been established:

    D⇐⋀k∈VkD \Leftarrow \bigwedge_{k \in V} k

    In plain language:

    Destruction requires proof of the preceding required states.

    This formalization is intentionally simple. Its value is conceptual clarity rather than mathematical novelty.

    27. The Method as a Meta-Language

    The most speculative—and potentially most interesting—extension of the philosophy is to treat the routine contract itself as a small meta-language.

    A routine can be described independently of implementation:

    ROUTINE:
    Verify Webpage

INPUT:
    SESSION_NAME
    PAGE_URL

PRECONDITIONS:
    Web repository already verified

ACTION:
    Request PAGE_URL

VERIFY:
    HTTP success
    HTML content present

FAILURE:
    Stop

SUCCESS:
    Permit next routine

    A human can understand this.

    A programmer can implement it.

    An AI can reason about it.

    A reviewer can audit it.

    A testing system can potentially derive tests from it.

    That suggests a broader possibility:

    A sufficiently explicit routine contract may serve as an intermediate representation between human intent and executable software.

    This proposition deserves experimentation.

    28. Potential Future Research

    Several questions emerge from the method.

    Research Question 1

    Does explicit routine contracting reduce defects in AI-assisted programming?

    Research Question 2

    Does separating action from verification improve debugging speed?

    Research Question 3

    Does a simple orchestration layer reduce maintenance complexity?

    Research Question 4

    Can routine contracts be automatically transformed into test specifications?

    Research Question 5

    Can AI systems produce more reliable code when required to satisfy explicit routine contracts?

    Research Question 6

    Can the method be generalized beyond shell automation?

    Potential environments include:

    • Python;

    • JavaScript;

    • infrastructure automation;

    • scientific workflows;

    • data pipelines;

    • laboratory procedures;

    • archival systems;

    • deployment systems;

    • and AI-agent workflows.

    These should be treated as research questions rather than assumed conclusions.

    29. Addendum A — The "Boring Routine" Principle

    The phrase "make the routines boring" deserves special emphasis.

    A routine becomes dangerous when it begins accumulating unrelated intelligence.

    For example:

    VERIFY WEBPAGE

    should not become:

    VERIFY WEBPAGE
IF FAILURE TRY THREE OTHER URLS
IF THAT FAILS REBUILD THE PAGE
IF THAT FAILS CHANGE THE REPOSITORY
IF THAT FAILS DELETE TEMPORARY FILES
IF THAT FAILS TRY AGAIN TOMORROW

    The resulting program may appear sophisticated.

    It is actually difficult to reason about.

    A boring routine has a smaller behavioral surface.

    That makes its failure modes easier to understand.

    30. Addendum B — The Stop Rule

    The architecture benefits from a universal rule:

    If a required checkpoint fails, stop the chain unless the architecture explicitly defines a recovery routine.

    This distinction is important.

    Recovery should not be accidental.

    If recovery is desired, it should itself become a named routine with its own contract.

    For example:

    08 VERIFY WEB
       ↓
    FAILURE
       ↓
08R RECOVER WEB
       ↓
08 VERIFY WEB AGAIN

    The recovery mechanism is therefore visible.

    It does not hide inside verification.

    31. Addendum C — The Evidence Ladder

    The architecture can also be understood as an evidence ladder.

    LEVEL 1
"I attempted it."

LEVEL 2
"The local result exists."

LEVEL 3
"The remote repository contains it."

LEVEL 4
"The public service exposes it."

LEVEL 5
"The relationship between artifacts is verified."

LEVEL 6
"Only now is destructive cleanup permitted."

    Different systems may require different levels.

    The important principle is to name the level of evidence actually established.

    32. Addendum D — Research Archive Application

    The method has particular relevance to archives of human-AI research.

    A preserved research session may contain:

    questions
observations
definitions
hypotheses
arguments
experiments
programs
corrections
revisions
conclusions

    If the session is preserved only as a final document, much of the reasoning path disappears.

    Preserving the session as a primary artifact makes the development history available.

    The archive can then distinguish:

    WHAT WAS SAID
WHAT WAS PROPOSED
WHAT WAS TESTED
WHAT WAS VERIFIED
WHAT REMAINS HYPOTHETICAL

    This distinction is essential for responsible research provenance.

    33. Addendum E — Application to Human-AI Programming

    The architecture may also provide a useful discipline for AI-assisted development.

    Instead of asking an AI:

    "Write the program that does all of this."

    the human can provide:

    Routine 01
Purpose:
Input:
Preconditions:
Action:
Verification:
Failure:
Return:

    The AI then generates one bounded implementation.

    The human reviews it.

    The next routine is developed separately.

    This creates smaller units of agreement between human and machine.

    The AI does not need to infer the entire system simultaneously.

    The human does not need to inspect an enormous block of generated code to determine whether one small requirement was misunderstood.

    This could potentially make AI-assisted programming more auditable.

    Again, this is a proposed research direction rather than an established empirical conclusion.

    34. Conclusion

    The Checkpointed Routine Method begins with a simple idea:

    A complicated process does not require a complicated controller.

    Complexity can instead be distributed into small, explicit, independently understandable routines.

    Each routine:

    receives
prechecks
acts
verifies
returns

    The Hub:

    calls
checks
continues
or stops

    The system progresses only when its required checkpoints have been satisfied.

    Original artifacts are preserved before derivatives are created.

    Publication is separated from preservation.

    Verification is separated from action.

    Destruction is delayed until the evidence is sufficient.

    Failures stop the process rather than being quietly rationalized away.

    The resulting architecture is intentionally conservative.

    Its goal is not to make automation appear intelligent.

    Its goal is to make automation understandable, inspectable, recoverable, and trustworthy.

    The Session Preservation Wizard provides a concrete case study, but the underlying philosophy is broader.

    The deepest principle may be the simplest:

    Do not make the program clever. Make the structure clear.

    And perhaps the most useful operational expression of that principle is:

    Make the routines boring.

    A boring routine is easy to understand.

    An understandable routine is easier to test.

    A tested routine is easier to trust.

    A sequence of such routines can perform surprisingly sophisticated work without becoming a mysterious machine.

    That is the proposed foundation of the Checkpointed Routine Method.

    Appendix 1 — Canonical Routine Template

    ROUTINE XX — NAME

PURPOSE:
    What does this routine accomplish?

INPUT:
    What information does it receive?

PRECONDITIONS:
    What must already be true?

ACTION:
    What does it do?

VERIFICATION:
    How does it establish success?

FAILURE:
    What does failure mean?
    What must remain untouched?

RETURN:
    0 = SUCCESS
    non-zero = FAILURE

    Appendix 2 — Canonical Hub Pattern

    START

CALL ROUTINE 01
IF FAILURE → STOP

CALL ROUTINE 02
IF FAILURE → STOP

CALL ROUTINE 03
IF FAILURE → STOP

...

CALL ROUTINE N
IF FAILURE → STOP

SUCCESS

END

    The Hub should remain intentionally simple.

    Appendix 3 — Architectural Vocabulary

    Hub
    The controller that determines sequence and responds to routine results.

    Routine
    A bounded operation with a defined responsibility and contract.

    Checkpoint
    A condition that must be established before progression.

    Verification
    An operation that establishes whether a desired state actually exists.

    Primary artifact
    The original material being preserved.

    Derived artifact
    A transformed or adapted representation created for another purpose.

    Provenance
    The documented relationship and history connecting artifacts and actions.

    Progressive commitment
    The movement from reversible operations toward irreversible operations.

    Destructive operation
    An action that removes or permanently alters recoverable state.

    Failure state
    A condition in which the required success predicate has not been established.

    Terminal success
    The final state reached only after all required checkpoints have succeeded.

    Appendix 4 — The Session Preservation Wizard

    The case-study architecture can be summarized as:

    THUMB DRIVE
     │
     ▼
01 RECEIVE
     │
     ▼
02 VERIFY INPUT
     │
     ▼
03 ARCHIVE
     │
     ▼
04 PREPARE WEB COPY
     │
     ├──────────────► 05 PUSH LIBRARY
     │                       │
     │                       ▼
     │                 06 VERIFY LIBRARY
     │
     ▼
07 PUSH WEB
     │
     ▼
08 VERIFY WEB FILES
     │
     ▼
09 VERIFY ACTUAL WEBPAGE
     │
     ▼
10 CREATE LIBRARY LINK
     │
     ▼
11 VERIFY LIBRARY LINK
     │
     ▼
12 CLEAN TEMPORARY ARCHIVE
     │
     ▼
13 CLEAN THUMB DRIVE
     │
     ▼
★ MISSION ACCOMPLISHED ★

    The architecture deliberately maintains:

    LIBRARY
    = preservation

WEB
    = publication

READ_EPISODE
    = relationship

ARCHIVE
    = temporary safety state

THUMB DRIVE
    = incoming work state

    Appendix 5 — Proposed Evaluation Criteria

    If the method is eventually evaluated experimentally, useful measurements might include:

    • time required to locate the source of a failure;

    • number of unintended side effects;

    • time required for a new programmer to understand a routine;

    • number of assumptions that remain implicit;

    • ease of replacing an individual routine;

    • frequency of accidental destructive operations;

    • success rate of AI-generated routine implementations;

    • human ability to detect specification violations;

    • and recovery time following simulated failures.

    Such experiments would allow claims about the method's effectiveness to be tested rather than merely asserted.

    Final Statement

    This paper proposes a philosophy of automation in which clarity is treated as a functional property.

    The objective is not merely to make software execute.

    The objective is to make the execution understandable enough that humans can know:

    what happened,
what was verified,
what was not verified,
what remains safe,
and what may safely happen next.

    That may be the most important property of all in systems whose purpose is to preserve knowledge.

    I think this is a good Version 1.0 foundation for the Wizard. The next step should not be to immediately code the Hub. I would first treat this paper as the specification against which we review the thirteen routines, because that gives us a clean test: does every routine actually obey the philosophy we just wrote down?

    That review may reveal a few places where the existing routines need tightening before we freeze the Wizard.
